classification.difficultyReason: Rearranging quartics into a tangent identity includes a scaled reciprocal substitution and checking that division preserves roots.

content.prompt: Solve the following. You may assume the identity $\tan4\theta=\dfrac{4\tan\theta-4\tan^3\theta}{1-6\tan^2\theta+\tan^4\theta}$.

answer.short:
$x=\tan\left(\frac{\pi}{16}\right),\ \tan\left(\frac{5\pi}{16}\right),\ \tan\left(\frac{9\pi}{16}\right),\ \tan\left(\frac{13\pi}{16}\right)$.

Rearrange the substituted quartic to obtain $\tan4\theta=1$.
answer.worked:
Let $x=\tan\theta$.
$$\begin{align*}\tan^4\theta+4\tan^3\theta-6\tan^2\theta-4\tan\theta+1&=0\\1-6\tan^2\theta+\tan^4\theta&=4\tan\theta-4\tan^3\theta.\end{align*}$$
The denominator of the supplied identity is nonzero at a root: otherwise its numerator would also be zero, requiring $\tan\theta=0,1$ or $-1$, none of which makes the denominator zero. Thus
$$\begin{align*}\tan4\theta&=1\\4\theta&=\frac{\pi}{4}+k\pi\\\theta&=\frac{\pi}{16}+\frac{k\pi}{4},\quad k\in\mathbb Z.\end{align*}$$
For $k=0,1,2,3$, the four distinct roots are
$$x=\tan\left(\frac{\pi}{16}\right),\quad\tan\left(\frac{5\pi}{16}\right),\quad\tan\left(\frac{9\pi}{16}\right),\quad\tan\left(\frac{13\pi}{16}\right).$$
These exhaust the roots of the quartic.

answer.short:
$x=2\cot\left(\frac{\pi}{16}\right),\ 2\cot\left(\frac{5\pi}{16}\right),\ 2\cot\left(\frac{9\pi}{16}\right),\ 2\cot\left(\frac{13\pi}{16}\right)$.

Rewrite the substituted equation in $\tan\theta$ to obtain $\tan4\theta=1$.
answer.worked:
Let $x=2\cot\theta$.
$$\begin{align*}16\cot^4\theta-64\cot^3\theta-96\cot^2\theta+64\cot\theta+16&=0\\\cot^4\theta-4\cot^3\theta-6\cot^2\theta+4\cot\theta+1&=0.\end{align*}$$
Since $x=0$ is not a root, $\cot\theta\ne0$. Multiply by $\tan^4\theta$:
$$\begin{align*}1-4\tan\theta-6\tan^2\theta+4\tan^3\theta+\tan^4\theta&=0\\1-6\tan^2\theta+\tan^4\theta&=4\tan\theta-4\tan^3\theta.\end{align*}$$
The denominator of the supplied identity cannot vanish here: simultaneous zero numerator would require $\tan\theta=0,1$ or $-1$, whose denominator values are $1,-4,-4$. Therefore
$$\begin{align*}\tan4\theta&=1\\4\theta&=\frac{\pi}{4}+k\pi\\\theta&=\frac{\pi}{16}+\frac{k\pi}{4},\quad k\in\mathbb Z.\end{align*}$$
For $k=0,1,2,3$,
$$x=2\cot\left(\frac{\pi}{16}\right),\quad2\cot\left(\frac{5\pi}{16}\right),\quad2\cot\left(\frac{9\pi}{16}\right),\quad2\cot\left(\frac{13\pi}{16}\right).$$
These four values are defined and distinct, so they exhaust the roots of the quartic.
